body.text: Building on Senior 2's factorising (Algebra 2), the quadratic formula solves any quadratic equation ax^2+bx+c=0, even when it doesn't factorise neatly.

Solve x^2 - 3x + 4 = 0 using the formula, where a=1, b=-3, c=4: x = (3 ± √(9-16)) / 2. Since 9-16 = -7 is negative, there is no real square root, so this equation has no real solutions — its graph never crosses the x-axis.

Solve x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0 using completing the square: x^2 - 5x = -6, add (5/2)^2=6.25 to both sides: x^2-5x+6.25 = 0.25, so (x-2.5)^2 = 0.25, x-2.5 = ±0.5, giving x=3 or x=2 — matching the factorised answer (x-2)(x-3)=0 from Senior 2.

The roots of a quadratic equation are exactly where its graph crosses the x-axis. A graph that touches the x-axis at one point (a repeated root) has b^2-4ac=0; a graph that doesn't cross the x-axis at all (no real roots) has b^2-4ac<0, matching the x^2-3x+4 example above.

Use the PhET Graphing Quadratics simulation to change a, b and c in y = ax^2+bx+c and watch the parabola and its roots move — a fast way to see how the discriminant b^2-4ac controls whether a quadratic has two, one, or no real roots.
